strengths: The controlled methodology is a genuine advance over prior coarse approaches: by machine-translating the same evidence documents into multiple languages and varying only the language of the cited document while holding content, relevance, query, and document positions fixed, the authors credibly isolate the effect of language on citation behavior (§3.2).

Using model internals (next-token citation-ID prediction and logit lens) provides a finer-grained and less hallucination-prone measurement than comparing citation frequencies against document-language distributions, and the decision-point analysis (around layer 22 for LLaMA-3.1 8B) offers a mechanistic view of when language preference is committed.

The empirical evaluation is broad and internally consistent: 8 languages spanning resource levels and scripts, 6 open-weight models of varying size/family, statistically tested with Bonferroni correction, and the English-preference pattern replicates across all models and target languages (Table 1).

The robustness checks strengthen the claims: an alternative MT system (TOWER-INSTRUCT, Table 11), contributive attribution via ContextCite (Table 12, Figure 19), entropy/probability analysis (Tables 6–7), a two-step citation filtering pipeline validated by human annotation, and the query-language and relevance-vs-language experiments.

Reproducibility is reasonable: open-weight models with HuggingFace identifiers, public datasets (ELI5/WebGPT, MIRACL), full prompts in Appendix A, and documented human annotation with fair compensation ($16/hour via Prolific).

The relevance-vs-language result (§7, Figure 5/Table 9) — that an irrelevant English distractor degrades citation more than a relevant non-English document — is a practically important finding for building more robust and equitable mRAG systems, and the limitations section honestly scopes the synthetic setup.
weaknesses: The core metric conflates 'preference' with 'capability': lower next-token accuracy when the cited document is in a non-English language may reflect weaker language-specific processing rather than a systematic preference to cite English. The paper does not fully disentangle these, though the ContextCite and entropy analyses partially mitigate this concern.

The machine-translation confound is not fully resolved. Lower-resource languages have lower MT quality, and the alternative MT experiment (Table 11) actually shows larger English gaps that track MT quality (Arabic is worst in both TOWER and Google setups). The argument that resource level rather than MT quality drives preference (Appendix D.1) is plausible but not conclusive.

The final evaluation pool is small (792 statements from 270 queries), so per-language/per-model cells and the position-bin analyses (Figure 2) may be noisy and underpowered; statistical significance does not preclude sensitivity to the specific o3-generated reference reports.

The relevance-vs-language conclusion is inferred from relative accuracy drops in a simplified setting with exactly one relevant and one irrelevant document (§7). Alternative explanations — distractor salience, position effects, or shared-script plausibility (the authors themselves raise this for Swahili) — are not ruled out.

The synthetic MT-based setup and the use of o3 as the reference-report generator mean the 'correct' citation is defined by one model's output; while judge-majority voting and NLI filtering help, statements with multiple valid supporting documents may be systematically mislabeled.

Ecological validity is limited: retrieval is assumed complete and all documents equally relevant in the main experiments, and real mRAG retrieval noise, code-switching, and natively authored (non-translated) non-English documents are not represented.

strengths: Novel, controlled methodology: measuring language preference via next-token prediction of the correct citation ID while holding document content constant through parallel translation is a genuine advance over prior frequency-counting and embedding-similarity proxies, and it directly addresses the confounds (C1, C2) the paper identifies.

Comprehensive experimental scope: 8 languages spanning different resource levels, families, scripts, and typologies, crossed with 6 open-weight models of varying scale and multilinguality, plus several complementary analyses (position bias, layer-wise logit lens, query-language variants, relevance-vs-language, corroborative vs contributive attribution via ContextCite, and an alternative MT system).

The central English-preference finding is robust and supported by converging evidence: consistent, statistically significant accuracy drops across all models and languages (Table 1), higher next-token probability and lower entropy for English (Tables 6-7), logit-lens showing incorrect predictions are English IDs (Figure 3), and ContextCite showing greater reliance on English sources (Table 12).

Careful validation and robustness work: a stratified human annotation study validating the LLM-as-judge + NLI filter (Krippendorff's alpha 0.559; supported 4.15 vs unsupported 2.49), reporting of COMET-QE translation quality, and replication with TOWER-INSTRUCT translations; prompts and dataset statistics are provided.
Honest limitations section that openly states the simplifying assumptions (complete retrieval, pairwise-vs-English comparisons, simulated mRAG via MT) rather than hiding them.
Ethical treatment of human annotation (Prolific annotators paid $16/hour, US-based, power analysis for sample size) is appropriate.
weaknesses: The central construct is not cleanly identified: 'preference' is defined operationally as a citation-accuracy gap, but this gap also reflects cross-lingual grounding capability (the model may simply fail to link an English statement to a foreign-language source). The logit-lens and ContextCite analyses partially mitigate this but do not disentangle 'cannot use foreign documents' from 'prefers English,' which undercuts the strong 'preference' framing.

The main comparison (Table 1) confounds the language of the cited document with context homogeneity: the English condition is a fully English context, whereas target-language conditions are mixed contexts. The measured Δ therefore partly reflects monolingual-consistency effects rather than language preference per se; the four-variant design in Section 6 addresses this, but the headline experiment does not control for it.

Machine-translation confound: evidence documents are translated English text with low COMET-QE scores (0.511 for Arabic, 0.516 for Swahili). The argument that MT quality does not drive the effect is correlational and weak, and the TOWER-INSTRUCT replication produces even larger gaps alongside extremely poor Arabic COMET (0.311), so translation artifacts cannot be ruled out as a driver.

Section 7 overclaims: the text states accuracies 'consistently drop below the baseline,' but Table 9 contradicts this (LLaMA-3.1 8B: Korean 0.952, Russian 0.965, Swahili 0.974 all exceed the 0.944 En-En baseline). Effect sizes are also tiny on a near-ceiling baseline (~94%), and the experiment uses a different dataset (MIRACL) with a nearly trivial task, so the headline claim that 'language outweighs relevance' is not well supported.

The evaluation measures agreement with a single generator's (o3) citation choices rather than objective correctness: statements are filtered to those where a majority of judges select the cited document, but multiple documents may legitimately support a statement, so models citing a different (often English) document are penalized and this is then interpreted as preference.

Statistical treatment is incomplete: two-sided t-tests treat statement-level observations as independent, ignoring clustering within queries; no confidence intervals or effect sizes are reported; and the final verified pool (792 statements) is modest for the per-language breakdowns.

No direct comparison against the prior preference measures (frequency-based, embedding-similarity, information-overlap) is provided to demonstrate that the new controlled method yields different or additional insight, leaving the claimed methodological advantage largely asserted.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and well-motivated problem — language preference in long-form multilingual RAG — and correctly identifies that prior measurements (citation frequency vs. document language distribution, information overlap, embedding similarity) are confounded by relevance/informativeness and citation hallucination. The framing of the two confounds (C1, C2) is clear and the proposed solution targets them directly.

The core methodological idea is elegant and genuinely novel: by translating the same evidence document into multiple languages and holding all other documents, positions, and the query fixed, the authors isolate the effect of language using model-internal next-token accuracy on the citation ID. This is a more controlled measurement than prior citation-frequency or embedding-similarity proxies, and it directly measures the model's citation decision rather than a downstream correlate.

The empirical scope is strong and supports generality claims: eight languages spanning high/mid/low resource levels, different families, scripts, and typologies, plus six open-weight models varying in scale (8B–70B), family, and degree of multilinguality. The consistent English-preference pattern across all model-language pairs is convincing.

The paper goes well beyond a single headline result. The amplifying factors (lower-resource languages, mid-context position), the layer-wise logit-lens analysis showing a decision point and persistence, the query-language experiments, the relevance-vs-language trade-off experiment, and the contributive-attribution analysis with ContextCite collectively give a multi-angle picture of the phenomenon rather than a one-off measurement.

Robustness and validation are handled thoughtfully: a human annotation study (with a power analysis and inter-annotator agreement reported) validates the LLM-as-judge + NLI filtering pipeline; the main result is replicated with an alternative MT system (TOWER-INSTRUCT) with all gaps still significant; and COMET-QE scores are reported to argue that MT quality does not drive the resource-level trend.

The limitations section is honest and specific about the simplifying assumptions (complete retrieval, pairwise-vs-English comparisons, MT-simulated multilinguality), and the paper provides all prompts in the appendix, uses open-weight models, and releases enough detail to enable partial reproduction.
weaknesses: Conceptual ambiguity between 'preference' and differential capability. The measured quantity is the accuracy gap in predicting the correct citation ID when a document is in a given language. A model that simply has weaker internal representations for Swahili than English will show a large gap without 'preferring' English in any behavioral sense. The paper frames the effect as a preference/bias throughout but does not cleanly disentangle 'systematically favors' from 'is worse at using.' The relevance-vs-language experiment (Section 7) is the strongest evidence for a genuine preference, but even there an alternative explanation — that English distractors are more salient/confusable — is acknowledged rather than ruled out. The Section 6 finding that models do best with a query-language cited document in an otherwise-English context further suggests a contrast/salience mechanism rather than pure English preference, which sits somewhat uneasily with the paper's central narrative.

Translation confound is only partially resolved. All non-English documents are machine-translated, and COMET-QE scores differ substantially by language (e.g., Arabic 0.511 and Swahili 0.516 vs. French 0.566 for documents). The authors argue resource level correlates better than MT quality, but the correlation is imperfect and the argument is correlational; the alternative-MT experiment shows the trend persists but with different per-language rankings (Arabic becomes the worst), which actually complicates the resource-level story. A more decisive control (e.g., human-translated or back-translated subsets, or matching MT quality across languages) is missing.

Proxy validity for long-form citation behavior. Preference is measured via a forced, single-sentence prompt ending in '[' and next-token accuracy on a digit. Whether this reflects the citation decisions the model would actually make in free-form long-form generation (the setting the paper claims to study) is not directly established. The connection between the internal next-token metric and real citation behavior in unconstrained generation is assumed rather than validated.

Small effective dataset and limited statistical power for fine-grained claims. The final pool is 792 statements from 270 ELI5 queries restricted to K<10 documents. Once sliced by language × position (first/middle/last) × model, per-cell sample sizes become small, yet the paper makes position-amplification claims from these bins. The MIRACL relevance experiment (231 queries, one relevant + one irrelevant doc) yields very high accuracies (e.g., 0.94+ for LLaMA-3.1 8B), which raises questions about the discriminative headroom and the robustness of the 'trade-off' conclusions.

Reproducibility is constrained by reliance on proprietary components. Google Translate API for all translations and proprietary judge/generator models (OpenAI o3, o4-mini, Gemini 2.5 Pro) for report generation and filtering make exact reproduction difficult, and these components may change over time. The context-window/dataset construction pipeline is also complex, so small changes could shift the statement pool.

Some presentation issues: the extracted manuscript shows mangled figure captions and a duplicated paragraph in Appendix D.4 (the LLaMA-3.3 70B description is repeated verbatim), and several figure legends (e.g., Figure 5, Figure 19) are hard to parse from the text alone. These suggest the final formatting needs attention, though they may partly be artifacts of extraction.
